source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 15 (PDF 45-60, printed 1-16); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 15 (Physical Optics), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 The wave nature of light was first proposed in 1678 by:
blocks.explanation: The wave nature of light was first proposed in 1678 by Christiaan Huygens (introduction).

book_ref.quote: The wave nature of light was first proposed in 1678 by Christiaan Huygens

blocks.prompt: 2 At the time of Huygens, the more famous and accepted theory of light was:
blocks.explanation: Evidence for the wave theory was not convincing then, so Newton's corpuscular theory (1672) was more famous and accepted (introduction).

book_ref.quote: the Newton's theory about the corpuscular nature of light in 1672, was more famous and accepted

blocks.prompt: 3 Which experiment, performed in 1801, proved the wave nature of light?
blocks.explanation: Young's interference experiment of 1801 proved the wave nature of light and established Huygens' wave theory (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Young's interference experiment performed in 1801 proved wave nature of light

blocks.prompt: 4 According to the chapter, Maxwell (1860) considered light to be:
blocks.explanation: In 1860 Maxwell considered light to be electromagnetic waves (introduction).

book_ref.quote: In 1860, Maxwell considered light to be the electromagnetic waves.

blocks.prompt: 5 In Maxwell's picture, electromagnetic waves are produced by:

options.text: a uniform current in a straight wire

blocks.explanation: Oscillating electric charges produce changing electric and magnetic fields that regenerate each other and can travel through vacuum (introduction).

book_ref.quote: the oscillating electric charges can produce changing electric and magnetic fields

blocks.prompt: 6 The quantum mechanical explanation of the early twentieth century showed that light has:

options.text: a dual nature, both wave and particle

blocks.explanation: Quantum mechanics revealed the dual nature of light: wave and particle characteristics, depending on the experiment (introduction).

book_ref.quote: the quantum mechanical explanation revealed the dual nature of light

blocks.prompt: 7 Light interacts with matter as discrete, massless particles called:
blocks.explanation: Light propagates as an electromagnetic wave but interacts with matter as massless particles called photons (introduction).

book_ref.quote: interacts with matter as discrete, massless particles called photons

blocks.prompt: 8 Which pair of properties of light, studied in this chapter, is associated with its wave nature?
blocks.explanation: The chapter studies interference and diffraction, properties associated with the wave nature of light (introduction).

book_ref.quote: In this chapter we will study the properties of light, associated with its wave nature

blocks.prompt: 9 A wavefront is an imaginary surface joining all points where the waves have the same:
blocks.explanation: A wavefront connects all the points where the waves have the same phase (15.1).

book_ref.quote: A wavefront is an imaginary surface that connects all the points where the waves have the same phase.

blocks.prompt: 10 Light reaching us from a distant star has wavefronts that are:
blocks.explanation: Light waves from distant stars are given as an example of plane wavefronts (15.1).

book_ref.quote: Plane wave fronts: Represented as a straight line like light waves from the distant stars

blocks.prompt: 11 Waves spreading out on the water of a pond from a disturbance at one point form:
blocks.explanation: Circular wavefronts are formed in water inside a pond (15.1).

book_ref.quote: Circular wavefronts: Represented by circles as formed in water inside a pond.

blocks.prompt: 12 A point source of sound in open three-dimensional space produces:

options.text: circular wavefronts in a plane only

blocks.explanation: In three-dimensional space a point source gives spherical wavefronts that spread out in all directions (15.1).

book_ref.quote: Spherical wavefronts: Formed in three-dimensional space by a sound or light wave.

blocks.prompt: 13 Spherical wavefronts of sunlight can be taken as plane at the earth because:

options.text: the distance from the source is very large
the sun is a line source

blocks.explanation: At very large distances, as for light from the sun, the wavefronts can be assumed to be planes at the earth's surface (15.1).

book_ref.quote: For very large distances, like light rays coming from sun, these wavefronts can be assumed as planes

blocks.prompt: 14 Microwaves of wavelength 2.8 cm travel as plane wavefronts, each one wavelength from the next. The distance between the 1st and the 6th of these wavefronts is:
blocks.explanation: Successive wavefronts are one wavelength apart; from the 1st to the 6th there are 5 gaps: 5 × 2.8 cm = 14 cm (15.1).

book_ref.quote: The shortest distance between wavefronts is always equal to wavelength of wave.

blocks.prompt: 15 The direction in which a wave transfers energy is, relative to its wavefront:

options.text: at any angle depending on amplitude

blocks.explanation: The direction of transfer of energy is always perpendicular to the wavefront at every point (15.1).

book_ref.quote: Direction of transfer of energy of wave is always perpendicular to any point on the surface of a given wavefront.

blocks.prompt: 16 A line at right angles to a wavefront, showing its direction of travel, is called:
blocks.explanation: A line at right angles to a wavefront showing its direction of travel is a ray (15.1).

book_ref.quote: A line at right angle to a wavefront which shows its direction of travel is called a ray

blocks.prompt: 17 A straight vibrator (line source) in a ripple tank produces wavefronts that are:
blocks.explanation: A line source such as a vibrator in a ripple tank creates plane, straight wavefronts in two dimensions (15.1).

book_ref.quote: A line source for example a vibrator in a ripple tank creates a wavefronts that are plane

blocks.prompt: 18 Plane wavefronts of light can be obtained by placing a point source of light:

options.text: at the centre of a concave mirror's surface
at the focal point of a lens

blocks.explanation: If a source of light is placed at the focal point of a lens, plane wavefronts are formed on the other side (15.1).

book_ref.quote: If a source of light is placed at the focal point of a lens. Plane wavefronts are formed

blocks.prompt: 19 A periodic source produces a succession of wavefronts that are:
blocks.explanation: A periodic source produces a succession of wavefronts, all of the same shape (15.1).

book_ref.quote: If the source is periodic, it produces a succession of wavefronts, all of the same shape.

blocks.prompt: 20 Huygens' principle is a geometrical method for finding:

options.text: the speed of light in vacuum
the shape of a wavefront at a later time from its known shape now

blocks.explanation: From the known shape of a wavefront at one instant it finds the shape at some later time (15.2).

book_ref.quote: is a geometrical method for finding, from the known shape of a wavefront at some instant

blocks.prompt: 21 According to Huygens, every point of a wavefront acts as a source of:
blocks.explanation: Every point of a wavefront may be considered the source of secondary wavelets (15.2).

book_ref.quote: every point of a wavefront may be considered the source of secondary wavelets

blocks.prompt: 22 Huygens' secondary wavelets spread out with a speed:

options.text: equal to the speed of propagation of the wave
twice the speed of the wave
half the speed of the wave
equal to the speed of light always

blocks.explanation: The wavelets spread out in all directions with a speed equal to the speed of propagation of the wave (15.2).

book_ref.quote: spread out in all directions with a speed equal to the speed of propagation of the wave

blocks.prompt: 23 In Huygens' construction, the new wavefront is the surface:

options.text: through the centres of the wavelets
tangent to all the secondary wavelets (their envelope)

blocks.explanation: The new wavefront is the surface tangent to the secondary wavelets, called their envelope (15.2).

book_ref.quote: constructing a surface tangent to the secondary wavelets or, as it is called, the envelope of the wavelets

blocks.prompt: 24 A light wavefront moves through a medium at 2.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The radius of the Huygens' wavelets drawn for a time interval of 4.0 ns is:

book_ref.quote: Then in time t the wavefront travels a distance vt.

blocks.prompt: 25 A sound wavefront AB travels at 340 m s⁻¹. To draw its position 0.020 s later by Huygens' method, circles of radius ____ are drawn with centres on AB.

book_ref.quote: We construct several circles (traces of spherical wavelets) with radius vt, centered at points along AB.

blocks.prompt: 26 In the chapter's Huygens construction of the new wavefront CD, the speed of the wave is assumed to be:

options.text: greatest at the centre of AB
zero at the ends of AB

blocks.explanation: The construction assumes v, the speed of propagation, is the same at all points (15.2).

book_ref.quote: We assume that v, the speed of propagation of the wave, is the same at all points.

blocks.prompt: 27 The results of Huygens' principle can also be obtained from:
blocks.explanation: All results of Huygens' principle can also be obtained from Maxwell's equations, but Huygens' model is simpler to use (15.2).

book_ref.quote: All the results that we obtain from Huygens' Principle can also be obtained from Maxwell's equations

blocks.prompt: 28 Two sources are called coherent if the waves they emit have:

options.text: a phase difference that changes rapidly

blocks.explanation: Coherent sources emit waves that have a constant phase difference (coherence).

book_ref.quote: Coherent sources emit waves that have a constant phase difference.

blocks.prompt: 29 Two waves can have a constant phase difference only if their:

options.text: frequencies are the same and remain constant

blocks.explanation: A constant phase difference needs the same frequency that remains constant (coherence).

book_ref.quote: the two waves can only have a constant phase difference if their frequencies are the same and remains constant

blocks.prompt: 30 Two loudspeakers connected to different signal generators of slightly different frequencies give:

options.text: a fixed pattern of loud and quiet regions
loud, then soft, then loud sound, with the pattern shifting around the room

blocks.explanation: The waves start in phase but soon go out of phase, so the interference pattern keeps shifting (coherence).

book_ref.quote: If they were connected to different signal generators with slightly different frequencies

blocks.prompt: 31 Two loudspeakers act as coherent sources when they are:

options.text: connected to the same signal generator
connected to two generators of different frequency

blocks.explanation: Connecting both loudspeakers to the same signal generator keeps their waves constantly in phase (coherence).

book_ref.quote: By connecting the two loudspeakers to the same signal generator

blocks.prompt: 32 Two separate lasers of the same frequency are not used as the two sources in a double-slit experiment because:

options.text: their bursts of light cannot be guaranteed to stay in phase

blocks.explanation: Laser light is made of many separate bursts; bursts from two lasers will not always be in phase, so they are not coherent (coherence).

book_ref.quote: We cannot guarantee that these bursts from two lasers will always be in phase with one another.

blocks.prompt: 33 Coherent light sources for a double-slit experiment are obtained by:

options.text: using two bulbs of the same power
using two lasers of different colours
dividing the light of a single laser with two slits
using sunlight directly on the screen

blocks.explanation: A single laser's light divided by two slits makes the slits act as two coherent sources (coherence).

book_ref.quote: This problem is overcome by using a single laser and dividing its light using the two slits

blocks.prompt: 34 If the two sources were not coherent, the screen would show:

options.text: sharp fixed bright and dark fringes

blocks.explanation: The pattern would change far too fast for the eye, so only a uniform band of light is seen (coherence).

book_ref.quote: We would simply see a uniform band of light, without any definite bright and dark regions.

blocks.prompt: 35 An everyday example of interference of light given in the chapter is:

options.text: a shadow of a pole in sunlight
haloes around street lamps or the Moon on a foggy night
an image in a plane mirror
a rainbow seen only in a prism

blocks.explanation: Haloes of light around street lamps or the Moon on a foggy night are interference seen in everyday life (coherence).

book_ref.quote: you may have noticed haloes of light around street lamps or the Moon on a foggy night

blocks.prompt: 36 The pattern formed when two coherent waves meet, reinforcing at some points and cancelling at others, is called:
blocks.explanation: Two coherent waves reinforcing at some points and cancelling at others form a pattern called interference (15.3).

book_ref.quote: Two coherent waves, when meet in a region, they reinforce each other at some points

blocks.prompt: 37 Two waves each of amplitude 3 mm arrive at a point exactly in phase. The amplitude of the resultant wave is:
blocks.explanation: In phase with equal amplitude, the resultant has twice the amplitude of one wave: 2 × 3 = 6 mm (15.3).

book_ref.quote: The principle of superposition predicts that the resultant wave has twice the amplitude of a single wave.

blocks.prompt: 38 Two waves of equal amplitude 4 mm meet exactly in antiphase. The resultant amplitude is:
blocks.explanation: Equal amplitudes in antiphase cancel: destructive interference gives zero resultant (15.3, Fig. 15.3 b).

book_ref.quote: Blue and green waves of the same amplitude may give (a) constructive or (b) destructive interference

blocks.prompt: 39 Waves of amplitudes 2 units and 5 units meet in phase. The amplitude of the resultant wave is:
blocks.explanation: Waves of different amplitudes also interfere constructively; in phase the amplitudes add: 2 + 5 = 7 units (15.3).

book_ref.quote: waves of different amplitudes can also interfere constructively

blocks.prompt: 40 A sound wave can produce interference only with:
blocks.explanation: The waves must be of the same type; sound waves interfere only with sound waves (15.3).

book_ref.quote: Waves must be of same type i.e. sound waves can only produce interference with other sound waves.

blocks.prompt: 41 Which of these is one of the chapter's basic conditions for two waves to produce interference?

options.text: They must have exactly equal amplitudes
They must come from two separate lasers
They must move in the same or almost the same direction

blocks.explanation: The waves must be of the same type, coherent, and moving in the same or almost the same direction (15.3).

book_ref.quote: Waves must be moving in same or almost same direction.

blocks.prompt: 42 If two interfering waves have different amplitudes, then:

options.text: interference still occurs but the contrast of the pattern decreases
the dark regions become completely dark

blocks.explanation: Interference still occurs with different amplitudes, but the contrast between the regions decreases (15.3).

book_ref.quote: Two waves can produce interference if amplitudes are different but this will decrease the contrast

blocks.prompt: 43 Adding waves of different wavelengths and amplitudes produces:
blocks.explanation: Adding waves of different wavelengths and amplitudes results in complex waves (15.3).

book_ref.quote: Adding waves of different wavelengths and amplitudes results in complex waves.

blocks.prompt: 44 In the two-slit laser arrangement, the bright fringes are regions where light waves from the two slits arrive:
blocks.explanation: Bright fringes are regions where waves from the two slits arrive in phase: constructive interference (interference of light waves).

book_ref.quote: These bright dots are referred to as interference

blocks.prompt: 45 In the sound analogue of the light fringe pattern, a dark fringe corresponds to:
blocks.explanation: Bright fringes correspond to loud sound and dark fringes to quiet sound or silence (interference of light waves).

book_ref.quote: Bright fringes correspond to loud sound, dark fringes to quiet sound or silence.

blocks.prompt: 46 In the two-slit laser experiment, one slit is covered. A point that was at a dark fringe now:

options.text: becomes bright, as a broad band of light appears

blocks.explanation: With one slit the fringes disappear and a broad band (single-slit diffraction pattern) appears; the dark point becomes bright (interference of light waves).

book_ref.quote: carefully cover up one of the slits so that light from the laser is only passing through one slit

blocks.prompt: 47 The broad band of light seen when only one slit is open is:

options.text: an interference pattern of two slits
the diffraction pattern of a single slit

blocks.explanation: With one slit open, the broad band of light is the diffraction pattern produced by a single slit (interference of light waves).

book_ref.quote: This broad band of light is the diffraction pattern produced by a single slit.

blocks.prompt: 48 A laser is more convenient than a bright bulb for the double-slit experiment because its light is:

options.text: concentrated into a narrow, more intense beam

blocks.explanation: Laser light is concentrated into a narrow, more intense beam (interference of light waves).

book_ref.quote: a laser is much more convenient because the light is concentrated into a narrow, more intense beam

blocks.prompt: 49 In the simple laser two-slit arrangement, the separation of the two slits is about:
blocks.explanation: The slits are two clear lines on a black slide separated by a fraction of a millimetre (interference of light waves).

book_ref.quote: The slits are two clear lines on a black slide, separated by a fraction of a millimeter.

blocks.prompt: 50 The wavelength of the microwaves used in the chapter's interference demonstration is:
blocks.explanation: The demonstration uses microwave equipment of 2.8 cm wavelength (15.4).

book_ref.quote: Using 2.8 cm wavelength microwave equipment

blocks.prompt: 51 In the microwave interference experiment, the two coherent sources are:

options.text: two gaps in a metal barrier

blocks.explanation: One transmitter is directed at a double gap in a metal barrier; waves diffracted at the two gaps interfere (15.4).

book_ref.quote: The microwave transmitter is directed towards the double gap in a metal barrier.

blocks.prompt: 52 The microwaves spread out into the region beyond the two gaps because of:
blocks.explanation: The microwaves are diffracted at the two gaps and spread out into the region beyond (15.4).

book_ref.quote: The microwaves are diffracted at the two gaps so that they spread out into the region beyond

blocks.prompt: 53 A probe receiver in the microwave experiment shows a region of low intensity. This is a region of:
blocks.explanation: Low intensity regions are regions of destructive interference; high intensity regions are constructive (15.4).

book_ref.quote: By moving the probe around, it is possible to detect regions of high intensity

blocks.prompt: 54 To give an audible output, the microwave probe receiver may be connected to:
blocks.explanation: The probe may be connected to a meter, or to an audio amplifier and loudspeaker for an audible output (15.4).

book_ref.quote: The probe may be connected to a meter, or to an audio amplifier and loudspeaker to give an audible output.

blocks.prompt: 55 In the 2.8 cm microwave experiment, the probe is at a point where the path difference from the two gaps is 8.4 cm. The probe detects:
blocks.explanation: 8.4/2.8 = 3, a whole number of wavelengths, so constructive interference and high intensity (15.4; condition from 15.5).

book_ref.quote: it is possible to detect regions of high intensity (constructive interference)

blocks.prompt: 56 With the 2.8 cm microwaves, the path difference at a point of minimum intensity could be:
blocks.explanation: Minimum needs a half-integer number of wavelengths: 1.5 × 2.8 = 4.2 cm; the others are whole numbers of λ (15.4).

book_ref.quote: Microwaves can also be used to show interference effects

blocks.prompt: 57 Thomas Young performed his double slit experiment in 1801 to show:
blocks.explanation: Young used the experiment to show the wave nature of light (15.5).

book_ref.quote: He used this experiment to show the wave nature of light.

blocks.prompt: 58 For coherent sources in Young's experiment, the waves must also have:
blocks.explanation: A constant phase difference also means the waves must have the same wavelength (15.5).

book_ref.quote: This also means that the waves must have the same wavelength.

blocks.prompt: 59 At point A on the screen, directly opposite the midpoint of the slits, the path difference and fringe are:
blocks.explanation: A is equidistant from both slits: path difference zero, waves in phase, a bright fringe (15.5).

book_ref.quote: This point is directly opposite the midpoint of the slits.

blocks.prompt: 60 At the midpoint B of the first dark fringe, the two rays have a phase difference of:
blocks.explanation: At B the rays are in antiphase, a phase difference of 180° (15.5).

book_ref.quote: the two rays must be in antiphase (phase difference of 180°)

blocks.prompt: 61 Light of wavelength 640 nm is used in Young's experiment. The path difference at the midpoint of the first dark fringe is:
blocks.explanation: First dark fringe: path difference = λ/2 = 640/2 = 320 nm (15.5).

book_ref.quote: The path difference between the two rays of light must be half a wavelength

blocks.prompt: 62 At point C, the midpoint of the next bright fringe after the central one, the path difference is:
blocks.explanation: At C ray 1 travels an extra whole wavelength λ; the rays are in phase and give a bright fringe (15.5).

book_ref.quote: this time, it has travelled an extra distance equal to a whole wavelength

blocks.prompt: 63 To get r₂ − r₁ = d sin θ, Young's analysis assumes that:

options.text: the slits are wider than the screen
L is so large compared with d that the lines from S₁ and S₂ to P are nearly parallel

blocks.explanation: With L much larger than d, the lines from S₁ and S₂ to P are very nearly parallel, giving r₂ − r₁ = d sin θ (15.5).

book_ref.quote: the lines from S₁ and S₂ to P, are very nearly parallel

blocks.prompt: 64 In typical light experiments, the slit separation and slit-to-screen distance are about:

options.text: a few metres; a few millimetres
a few centimetres; a few centimetres
a few millimetres; a metre or more

blocks.explanation: The slit separation is typically a few millimetres while the screen may be a metre or more away (15.5).

book_ref.quote: the slit separation is typically a few millimeters, while the screen may be a meter or more away

blocks.prompt: 65 Two slits are 0.20 mm apart. The path difference r₂ − r₁ for a point at θ = 0.30° is about:

book_ref.quote: Where θ is the angle between a line from slits to screen and the normal to the plane of the slits

blocks.prompt: 66 Bright fringes in a two-slit pattern occur where:
blocks.explanation: Constructive interference: path difference an integer number of wavelengths, d sin θ = mλ (Eq. 15.2).

book_ref.quote: constructive interference (reinforcement) occurs at points where the path difference is an integer number of wavelengths

blocks.prompt: 67 Dark fringes in a two-slit pattern occur where the path difference is:
blocks.explanation: Destructive interference: d sin θ = (m + ½)λ, a half-integer number of wavelengths (two-slit interference).

book_ref.quote: at points for which the path difference is a half-integer number (m + ½) of wavelengths

blocks.prompt: 68 Light of wavelength 640 nm falls on two slits 0.16 mm apart. The angle of the first dark fringe (m = 0) is about:
blocks.explanation: sin θ = (0 + ½)λ/d = 0.5 × 640 × 10⁻⁹ / 0.16 × 10⁻³ = 0.0020, so θ = 0.11° (two-slit interference).

book_ref.quote: destructive interference (cancellation) occurs, forming dark regions on the screen

blocks.prompt: 69 The interference fringes in Young's experiment are:

options.text: bright and dark bands parallel to the slits

blocks.explanation: The pattern is a succession of bright and dark bands, parallel to the slits S₁ and S₂ (two-slit interference).

book_ref.quote: the pattern on the screen of Fig. 15.9 is a succession of bright and dark bands

blocks.prompt: 70 The distance yₘ of the mth bright band from the centre is related to its angle θₘ by:
blocks.explanation: From the geometry of Fig. 15.10, yₘ = L tan θₘ (Eq. 15.3).

book_ref.quote: Let yₘ be the distance from the center of the pattern

blocks.prompt: 71 The step yₘ = L sin θₘ (Eq. 15.4) is valid because:

options.text: θₘ is very small, so sin θₘ ≈ tan θₘ
sin θₘ = tan θₘ for every angle

blocks.explanation: yₘ is much smaller than L, so θₘ is very small and sin θₘ ≈ tan θₘ; the result is an approximation for small angles (two-slit interference).

book_ref.quote: In such experiments, the distances yₘ are often much smaller than the distance L

blocks.prompt: 72 The position of the mth bright band for small angles is:
blocks.explanation: Combining yₘ = L sin θₘ with d sin θₘ = mλ gives yₘ = mLλ/d (Eq. 15.5).

book_ref.quote: positions of mth bright band is given by

blocks.prompt: 73 Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on slits 0.30 mm apart; the screen is 1.5 m away. The fringe spacing is:

book_ref.quote: The distance between centers of

blocks.prompt: 74 With λ = 650 nm, d = 0.50 mm and L = 2.0 m, the centre of the 4th bright band (m = 4) is at a distance from the centre of:

book_ref.quote: Let θₘ be the corresponding value of θ; then

blocks.prompt: 75 In a two-slit experiment the slit separation d is halved, everything else kept the same. The fringe spacing becomes:
blocks.explanation: Δy = Lλ/d is inversely proportional to d; halving d doubles the spacing (two-slit interference).

book_ref.quote: The distance between adjacent bright bands in the pattern is inversely proportional to the distance d

blocks.prompt: 76 Two-slit fringes on a screen 1.2 m away are 2.4 mm apart when the slits are 0.30 mm apart. The wavelength of the light is:

book_ref.quote: The closer together the slits are, the more the pattern spreads out.

blocks.prompt: 77 Light of wavelength 480 nm gives fringes 1.8 mm apart on a screen 1.5 m from two slits. The slit separation is:

book_ref.quote: When the slits are far apart, the bands in the pattern are closer together.

blocks.prompt: 78 The two-slit fringe equations are valid for:

options.text: any two sources, even if not coherent
any type of wave from two coherent sources, detected far away compared with d

blocks.explanation: The results are valid for any type of wave, if the resultant from two coherent sources is detected far away compared with d (two-slit interference).

book_ref.quote: the results given in Equation are valid for any type of wave

blocks.prompt: 79 The coloured bands seen on a thin layer of oil floating on water are due to:

options.text: interference of light reflected from the two surfaces of the film

blocks.explanation: Light reflected from the front and back surfaces of the thin film interferes (15.6).

book_ref.quote: We often see bright bands of color when light reflects from a thin layer of oil floating on water

blocks.prompt: 80 In a thin film of thickness t (Fig. 15.11), the second reflected wave is the one that:

options.text: passes through the upper surface and reflects from the lower surface
reflects from the upper surface only

blocks.explanation: Light transmitted through the upper surface is partly reflected at the lower surface (path abdef) (15.6).

book_ref.quote: Light transmitted through the upper surface is partly reflected at the lower surface (path abdef).

blocks.prompt: 81 A thin film in white light looks coloured because:

options.text: the film emits its own light
the film is a diffraction grating
interference is constructive for some wavelengths and destructive for others

blocks.explanation: Different colours have different wavelengths, so interference is constructive for some colours and destructive for others (15.6).

book_ref.quote: Different colors have different wavelengths, so the interference may be constructive for some colors

blocks.prompt: 82 The complex shapes of the coloured patterns on a soap bubble result from:

options.text: variations in the thickness of the film
variations in the speed of light in air
the shape of the light source

blocks.explanation: The complex shapes result from variations in the thickness of the film (15.6).

book_ref.quote: The complex shapes of the colored patterns result from variations in the thickness of the film.

blocks.prompt: 83 At nearly normal incidence, the path difference between the two waves reflected from an air wedge of thickness t is:
blocks.explanation: The path difference is just twice the thickness t of the air wedge at each point (15.6).

book_ref.quote: The path difference between the two waves is just twice the thickness t of the air wedge at each point.

blocks.prompt: 84 At a point of an air wedge where t = 0.45 μm, light of wavelength 600 nm has a path difference 2t equal to:

book_ref.quote: At points where 2t is an integer number of wave lengths, we expect to see constructive interference

blocks.prompt: 85 In the experiment with an air wedge between two glass plates, the line where the plates touch is seen as:
blocks.explanation: Along the line of contact a dark fringe is found, not a bright one (15.6).

book_ref.quote: Along the line where the plates are in contact, we find a dark fringe, not a bright one.

blocks.prompt: 86 The dark fringe at the line of contact of an air wedge shows that one reflected wave:

options.text: undergoes a half-cycle phase shift on reflection

blocks.explanation: One of the reflected waves has undergone a half-cycle phase shift during its reflection (15.6).

book_ref.quote: one or the other of the reflected waves has undergone a half cycle phase shift during its reflection

blocks.prompt: 87 The half-cycle phase shift on reflection can be predicted from:

options.text: Maxwell's equations and the electromagnetic nature of light

blocks.explanation: The phase shift can be predicted from Maxwell's equations and the electromagnetic nature of light (15.6).

book_ref.quote: this phase shift can be predicted from Maxwell's equations

blocks.prompt: 88 With the half-cycle phase shift, which points of an air wedge (light of wavelength λ) are dark?

options.text: Where 2t is a half-integer number of wavelengths
Only where t is very large
Where 2t is a whole number of wavelengths

blocks.explanation: The half-cycle shift interchanges bright and dark: the contact line (2t = 0) is dark, and so are points where 2t = mλ (15.6).

book_ref.quote: In that case the two waves that are reflected at the line of contact are a half-cycle out of phase

blocks.prompt: 89 Newton's rings are formed when:

options.text: a plano-convex lens is placed on a flat glass plate
two lasers shine on a screen

blocks.explanation: Newton's rings form when a plano-convex lens is placed on a flat glass plate, with a thin air film between them (15.7).

book_ref.quote: Newton's rings are formed when a plano-convex lens is placed on a flat glass plate

blocks.prompt: 90 Viewed in monochromatic light, the fringes of the lens and plate arrangement are:
blocks.explanation: Circular interference fringes are seen; they are called Newton's rings (15.7).

book_ref.quote: When we view the setup with monochromatic light, you see circular interference fringes

blocks.prompt: 91 A suitable monochromatic source for observing Newton's rings named in the chapter is:
blocks.explanation: Light from a monochromatic source such as a sodium lamp reflects from both surfaces of the air film (15.7).

book_ref.quote: Light from a monochromatic source (like a sodium lamp) reflects off both the top and bottom surfaces

blocks.prompt: 92 In Newton's rings, the thin film in which interference takes place is a film of:
blocks.explanation: A thin film of air is formed between the convex surface of the lens and the plane glass plate (15.7).

book_ref.quote: A thin film of air is formed between the two surfaces.

blocks.prompt: 93 Bright rings in Newton's rings are formed by:

options.text: constructive interference of the two reflected rays
destructive interference of the reflected rays

blocks.explanation: The reflected rays interfere constructively (bright rings) or destructively (dark rings) depending on path difference and phase shift (15.7).

book_ref.quote: The reflected rays interfere-constructively (bright rings)

blocks.prompt: 94 Which of the following is NOT a use of Newton's rings given in the chapter?

options.text: calculating the wavelength of monochromatic light
determining the radius of curvature of lenses
finding the interplanar spacing of crystals
detecting surface irregularities in precision optics

blocks.explanation: Newton's rings find wavelength, radius of curvature and surface irregularities; crystal spacing uses X-ray diffraction (15.7, 15.9).

book_ref.quote: helps determine the radius of curvature of lenses

blocks.prompt: 95 In precision optics, Newton's rings are used to detect:
blocks.explanation: Newton's rings are used in precision optics to detect surface irregularities (15.7).

book_ref.quote: used in precision optics to detect surface irregularities

blocks.prompt: 96 The bending of light around obstacles and its spreading into the geometrical shadow is called:
blocks.explanation: This property of light is called diffraction (15.8).

book_ref.quote: The property of bending of light around obstacles and spreading of light waves into the geometrical shadow

blocks.prompt: 97 Increasing the number of slits while keeping the spacing of adjacent slits constant makes the maxima:

options.text: stay in the same positions but become narrower

blocks.explanation: With more slits at the same spacing, the maxima are in the same positions but progressively narrower (15.8).

book_ref.quote: gives interference patterns in which the maxima are in the same positions, but progressively narrower

blocks.prompt: 98 A diffraction grating can measure wavelength to very high precision because its maxima are:
blocks.explanation: Because the maxima are so narrow, their angular position and hence the wavelength can be measured very precisely (15.8).

book_ref.quote: their angular position, and hence the wavelength, can be measured to very high precision

blocks.prompt: 99 A diffraction grating is:

options.text: an array of a large number of equally spaced parallel slits
a convex lens on a glass plate

blocks.explanation: An array of a large number of parallel slits with equal spacing between centres is a diffraction grating (15.8).

book_ref.quote: An array of a large number of parallel slits

blocks.prompt: 100 The first diffraction grating was constructed by Fraunhofer using:
blocks.explanation: The first grating was constructed by Fraunhofer using fine wires (15.8).

book_ref.quote: The first one was constructed by Fraunhofer using fine wires.

blocks.prompt: 101 Gratings can be made by:

options.text: scratching equally spaced grooves on glass or metal with a diamond point

blocks.explanation: Gratings are made by scratching equally spaced grooves with a diamond point, or by photographic reduction (15.8).

book_ref.quote: Gratings can be made by using a diamond point to scratch many equally spaced grooves

blocks.prompt: 102 For a grating, the slits are often called:
blocks.explanation: For a grating, slits are often called rulings or lines (15.8).

book_ref.quote: For a grating, what we have been calling slits are often called rulings or lines.

blocks.prompt: 103 The grating spacing d is:

options.text: the distance from grating to screen
the distance between the centres of adjacent slits
the total width of the grating

blocks.explanation: The spacing d between centres of adjacent slits is the grating spacing; the slit width is a different, smaller quantity (15.8).

book_ref.quote: The spacing d between centers of adjacent slits is called the grating spacing.

blocks.prompt: 104 Under far-field (Fraunhofer) conditions, the rays from a grating going to a particular point on the screen are taken as:
blocks.explanation: The screen is far enough away that all rays going to a particular point can be considered parallel (15.8).

book_ref.quote: We assume far-field (Fraunhofer) conditions

blocks.prompt: 105 The principal maxima of a diffraction grating are given by:
blocks.explanation: Maxima occur where the path difference for adjacent slits is an integer number of wavelengths: d sin θ = nλ (Eq. 15.7).

book_ref.quote: These are the directions for which the path difference for adjacent slits is an integer number of wavelengths.

blocks.prompt: 106 A grating has 500 lines per millimetre. Its grating spacing d is:

book_ref.quote: the value of d is the reciprocal of the number of slits per unit length

blocks.prompt: 107 Light of wavelength 600 nm falls normally on a grating of spacing 2.0 μm. The first-order line is at about:

book_ref.quote: the pattern is a series of very sharp lines at angles determined by this formula

blocks.prompt: 108 For the same grating (d = 2.0 μm) and λ = 600 nm, the second-order lines are at about:

book_ref.quote: The n = ±1 lines are called the first-order lines, the n = ±2 lines the second-order lines

blocks.prompt: 109 For the grating of spacing 2.0 μm with λ = 600 nm, the highest order that can be observed is:
blocks.explanation: sin θ cannot exceed 1, so n ≤ d/λ = 2000/600 = 3.33; the highest whole order is 3 (Eq. 15.7).

book_ref.quote: The angle for each wavelength is determined by Eq. (15.7) for a given value of n

blocks.prompt: 110 When a grating is illuminated by white light, each order n gives:
blocks.explanation: With white light, each value of n corresponds to a continuous spectrum in the pattern (15.8).

book_ref.quote: each value of n corresponds to a continuous spectrum in the pattern

blocks.prompt: 111 In the first-order spectrum of white light from a grating:

options.text: red light is deviated more than blue light
blue light is deviated more than red light
red light is not deviated at all

blocks.explanation: Longer wavelengths (red end) lie at larger angles than shorter wavelengths (blue end) (15.8).

book_ref.quote: long wavelengths (the red end of the spectrum) lie at larger angles

blocks.prompt: 112 For substantial deviation of light by a grating, the grating spacing d should be:

options.text: of the same order of magnitude as the wavelength

blocks.explanation: The sines of the angles are proportional to λ/d, so d should be of the same order as λ (15.8).

book_ref.quote: For substantial deviation to occur, the grating spacing d should be of the same order of magnitude

blocks.prompt: 113 Gratings for visible light usually have about 1000 slits per millimetre, so d is of the order of:
blocks.explanation: d is the reciprocal of slits per unit length: 1/1000 mm = 10⁻⁶ m = 1000 nm (15.8).

book_ref.quote: usually have about 1000 slits per millimeter

blocks.prompt: 114 A grating of 400 lines per mm is used with light of wavelength 500 nm. The second-order maximum is at about:

book_ref.quote: Fig. 15.16 is a cross section of a transmission grating

blocks.prompt: 115 The central maximum (n = 0) of a grating lies at:
blocks.explanation: For n = 0, d sin θ = 0, so θ = 0: the straight-ahead direction (Eq. 15.7).

book_ref.quote: an interference pattern is formed by the light that is transmitted through the slits

blocks.prompt: 116 Compared with a grating of 100 slits, a grating of 2000 slits with the same spacing gives spectral lines that are:
blocks.explanation: More slits at the same spacing make the maxima narrower, so the lines are sharper (15.8 and the Interesting Information box).

book_ref.quote: The spectrum of white light due to diffraction grating of 100 slits.

blocks.prompt: 117 The wavelength of X-rays is about:
blocks.explanation: X-rays are electromagnetic radiation of much shorter wavelength, about 10⁻¹⁰ m (15.9).

book_ref.quote: X-rays is a type of electromagnetic radiation of much shorter wavelength, about 10⁻¹⁰m.

blocks.prompt: 118 X-rays cannot be diffracted by an ordinary ruled grating but are diffracted by a crystal because:

options.text: the atomic spacing in a crystal (≈10⁻¹⁰ m) is of the order of the X-ray wavelength

blocks.explanation: Diffraction needs spacing of the order of the wavelength; the regular atoms of a crystal form a natural grating with spacing ≈10⁻¹⁰ m (15.9).

book_ref.quote: The regular array of atoms in a crystal forms a natural diffraction grating

blocks.prompt: 119 The study of the atomic structure of crystals by X-rays was started by:
blocks.explanation: The study was initiated by W.H. Bragg and W.L. Bragg (15.9).

book_ref.quote: The study of atomic structure of crystals by X-rays was initiated

blocks.prompt: 120 The Braggs found that a monochromatic X-ray beam was reflected from a crystal plane:

options.text: only after passing through a lens
as if the plane acted like a mirror

blocks.explanation: A monochromatic X-ray beam was reflected from a crystal plane as if it acted like a mirror (15.9).

book_ref.quote: They found that a monochromatic beam of X-rays was reflected from a crystal plane as if it acted like mirror.

blocks.prompt: 121 X-rays are incident at θ = 30° on atomic planes of spacing 0.25 nm. The path difference between beams reflected from adjacent planes is:
blocks.explanation: Path difference = 2d sin θ = 2 × 0.25 × sin 30° = 0.25 nm (15.9).

book_ref.quote: The effective path difference between the two reflected beams is 2d sinθ.

blocks.prompt: 122 Bragg's equation for reinforcement of X-rays reflected from crystal planes is:
blocks.explanation: The path difference 2d sin θ must be an integral multiple of λ: 2d sin θ = nλ (Eq. 15.8).

book_ref.quote: for reinforcement, the path difference should be an integral multiple of the wavelength

blocks.prompt: 123 In Bragg's equation 2d sin θ = nλ, n is called the:
blocks.explanation: The value of n is referred to as the order of reflection (15.9).

book_ref.quote: The value of n is referred to as the order of reflection.

blocks.prompt: 124 First-order Bragg reflection occurs at θ = 15° from planes of spacing 0.20 nm. The X-ray wavelength is about:

book_ref.quote: Suppose an X-rays beam is incident at an angle θ on one of the planes.

blocks.prompt: 125 X-rays of wavelength 0.10 nm give first-order Bragg reflection at 12°. The interplanar spacing is about:

book_ref.quote: It can be used to determine interplanar spacing between similar parallel planes of a crystal

blocks.prompt: 126 In Bragg reflection, the extra distance is travelled by the beam reflected from:
blocks.explanation: The beam reflected from the lower plane travels some extra distance compared with the beam from the upper plane (15.9).

book_ref.quote: The beam reflected from lower plane travels some extra distance

blocks.prompt: 127 In the Bragg derivation, d stands for:

options.text: the slit width of a grating
the constant spacing between parallel atomic planes

blocks.explanation: d is the constant interplanar spacing of atomic planes parallel to a crystal face (15.9).

book_ref.quote: a series of atomic planes of constant interplanar spacing d parallel to a crystal face

blocks.prompt: 128 X-ray diffraction has been used to find the structure of:

options.text: hemoglobin and the double helix of DNA

blocks.explanation: X-ray diffraction has been very useful in determining the structure of hemoglobin and the double helix of DNA (15.9).

book_ref.quote: determining the structure of biologically important molecules such as hemoglobin

blocks.prompt: 129 X-ray diffraction effects in a crystal arise from:

options.text: scattering of X-rays from the atoms in the crystal lattice
emission of light by the crystal

blocks.explanation: Scattering of X-rays from the atoms in a crystalline lattice gives diffraction effects similar to visible light on a grating (15.9).

book_ref.quote: The scattering of X-rays from the atoms in a crystalline lattice gives rise to diffraction effects
